lesson.title: Surveying the Keys: dict.keys()
lesson.summary: The keys() method returns a live view of every key in a dictionary, useful for membership tests and for seeing what fields are available.
lesson.body:
Sometimes you do not want a value out of a dictionary, you want to know what labels it uses in the first place. Maybe you received a dictionary of settings from another part of a program and need to check which options were actually provided. That is exactly what the keys() method is for: dictionary.keys() hands you every key currently stored in the dictionary.

What keys() returns is not a list, it is a special object called a dict_keys view. A view is like a live window into the dictionary rather than a frozen snapshot: if the dictionary changes after you grab the view, the view reflects those changes automatically the next time you look at it. Views are iterable, which means you can loop over them or test membership with in, and you can always wrap one in list() if you need an actual list, for example to sort it or index into it.

prices = {"pen": 1.5, "pencil": 0.5, "eraser": 0.75}
key_view = prices.keys()
print(key_view)
prices["marker"] = 2.0
print(key_view)
print("pen" in prices.keys())

This prints dict_keys(['pen', 'pencil', 'eraser']), then dict_keys(['pen', 'pencil', 'eraser', 'marker']), then True. Notice that key_view was created before "marker" was added, yet the second print shows "marker" anyway. That is the live part of a view in action: it did not copy the keys at creation time, it keeps watching the dictionary. The final line shows the most common real use of keys(): checking whether a particular key exists with the in operator, which reads naturally as 'is pen one of the keys.'

In practice, you rarely need to call .keys() just to test membership, because "pen" in prices works identically and is the more idiomatic style. Where keys() earns its place is when you want to loop over just the keys, compare the key sets of two dictionaries, or explicitly hand the set of keys to something else in your program.
